title: Vernier Callipers: diameter, internal diameter, depth and volume
objective: To measure the diameter of a small spherical and a cylindrical body using vernier callipers.
To measure the internal diameter and depth of a given beaker.
To calculate the volume of each body from the measured dimensions.

theory.statement: A vernier calliper carries an auxiliary sliding scale on which N divisions occupy the same length as (N − 1) divisions of the main scale. Because of this the vernier can resolve a fraction of a main scale division equal to 1/N of it, which is the least count of the instrument.
theory.derivationNote: If one main scale division is M.S.D., then N vernier divisions = (N − 1) M.S.D., so 1 vernier division = ((N − 1)/N) M.S.D. The difference between one main scale division and one vernier division is M.S.D. − ((N − 1)/N) M.S.D. = M.S.D./N. This difference is the least count: L.C. = 1 M.S.D. / N. With M.S.D. = 1 mm = 0.1 cm and N = 10, L.C. = 0.01 cm. The total reading is then M.S.R. + (coinciding vernier division × L.C.), from which any zero error must be subtracted algebraically.
keyEquations: Correct reading = Observed reading − zero error (with its own sign)

apparatus.name: Vernier callipers
apparatus.why: The measuring instrument; its two pairs of jaws read external and internal dimensions

apparatus.name: Spherical body
apparatus.why: External diameter measured between the lower (outside) jaws

apparatus.name: Cylindrical body
apparatus.why: External diameter and height measured to give the volume

apparatus.name: Beaker or calorimeter
apparatus.why: Internal diameter measured with the upper jaws, depth with the thin strip at the tail

apparatus.name: Magnifying lens
apparatus.why: Helps judge which vernier division exactly coincides with a main scale division

procedure.text: Determine the least count: note the value of one main scale division and count the number of divisions on the vernier scale. L.C. = 1 M.S.D. / N.
Bring the jaws into contact. If the vernier zero does not coincide with the main scale zero, note the zero error and its sign.
Place the sphere between the lower jaws and tighten them gently until the body is just gripped. Do not force the jaws.
Read the main scale division just before the vernier zero. This is the M.S.R.
Find the vernier division that exactly coincides with any main scale division. This is the V.S.R.
Calculate the observed reading as M.S.R. + V.S.R. × L.C., then apply the zero error correction.
Repeat the measurement in at least three mutually perpendicular directions, since the body may not be perfectly round.
Use the upper jaws to measure the internal diameter of the beaker and the thin strip at the tail to measure its depth.
Take the mean of the corrected readings and calculate the volume using the appropriate formula.

steps: Mean diameter d = Σ(corrected)/n, radius r = d/2
Volume from the appropriate formula for the shape

expectedResult.statement: The diameter of the given sphere is about 2.14 cm and its volume about 5.13 cm³, each measured to the least count of 0.01 cm.

safety: Tighten the jaws only until the body is just held; over-tightening damages both the instrument and a soft specimen.
Do not slide the vernier while the jaws grip the body, as this scratches the measuring faces.
Handle glass beakers carefully when inserting the depth strip.
Keep the calliper clean and dry; a grain of dust between the jaws is itself a zero error.
sourcesOfError: Zero error not noticed, or corrected with the wrong sign.
Backlash error: play between the sliding vernier and the main scale.
Parallax while judging which vernier division coincides.
The body not being perfectly spherical or cylindrical, so the diameter differs with direction.
Excessive pressure on the jaws compressing a soft body.
Reporting more significant figures than the least count justifies.

viva.question: What is the least count of a vernier calliper and how is it obtained?
viva.expectedConcept: The least count is the smallest length that can be measured, equal to one main scale division divided by the number of vernier divisions: L.C. = 1 M.S.D. / N. For M.S.D. = 1 mm and N = 10, L.C. = 0.01 cm.
viva.answerLogic: Must state the ratio, not merely quote 0.01 cm.
viva.commonMisconception: Quoting 0.01 cm as a fixed property of all vernier callipers rather than a consequence of M.S.D. and N.

viva.question: Why does a vernier scale have N divisions covering only (N − 1) main scale divisions?
viva.expectedConcept: So that each vernier division is shorter than a main scale division by exactly 1/N of it. That difference is what allows a fraction of a main scale division to be read.
viva.answerLogic: The vernier principle rests on the small, constant difference between the two divisions.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking the vernier simply magnifies the scale.

viva.question: What is positive zero error and how is it corrected?
viva.expectedConcept: When the jaws are closed, if the vernier zero lies to the RIGHT of the main scale zero the error is positive. The correction is to SUBTRACT it from every observed reading.
viva.answerLogic: Sign convention: correct reading = observed − zero error.
viva.commonMisconception: Adding a positive zero error instead of subtracting it.

viva.question: A calliper shows a negative zero error of 0.03 cm. The observed reading is 2.11 cm. What is the correct reading?
viva.expectedConcept: Correct reading = observed − (−0.03) = 2.11 + 0.03 = 2.14 cm. A negative zero error is added.
viva.answerLogic: Algebraic subtraction of a negative quantity.

viva.question: Why is the diameter measured in three mutually perpendicular directions?
viva.expectedConcept: A real body is not perfectly spherical. Measuring along different directions and taking the mean reduces the effect of this and of random error.
viva.commonMisconception: Believing repetition in the same direction is equally good.

viva.question: Which jaws are used to measure the internal diameter of a beaker?
viva.expectedConcept: The upper jaws, which open outwards against the inside wall of the vessel. The lower jaws are for external dimensions and the thin strip at the tail is for depth.
viva.answerLogic: Three separate measuring features of the instrument.
viva.commonMisconception: Using the lower jaws for internal measurement.

viva.question: What is backlash error and how do you avoid it?
viva.expectedConcept: It is caused by wear or play in the screw and slide, so the reading depends on the direction from which the jaws were moved. It is avoided by always turning the screw in one direction while taking a set of readings.
viva.answerLogic: A systematic error of mechanical origin.

viva.question: If you used a calliper with 50 vernier divisions instead of 10, what changes?
viva.expectedConcept: The least count improves from 0.01 cm to 0.002 cm, so the reading can be given to one more decimal place, but the instrument becomes harder to read and needs a lens.
viva.answerLogic: L.C. = M.S.D./N, so larger N means finer resolution.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking more divisions makes the measurement more accurate regardless of technique.

viva.question: Why should the result not be written as 2.1400 cm?
viva.expectedConcept: The instrument resolves only to 0.01 cm, so only two decimal places are meaningful. Extra digits imply a precision the instrument does not have.
viva.answerLogic: Significant figures must reflect the least count.
viva.commonMisconception: Copying all the digits from a calculator.

viva.question: Distinguish between accuracy and precision using this experiment.
viva.expectedConcept: Precision is how closely repeated readings agree, set here by the least count. Accuracy is how close the mean is to the true value, which an uncorrected zero error would destroy even if every reading agreed perfectly.
viva.answerLogic: Zero error affects accuracy, not precision.
viva.commonMisconception: Treating the two words as synonyms.

scientificValidation.formula: L.C. = M.S.D./N; reading = M.S.R. + V.S.R.×L.C. − zero error; V = (4/3)πr³ or πr²h
assumptions: The main scale is uniformly graduated
The jaws are true and undamaged
The body is gripped without deformation
Zero error is constant over the range used
scientificValidation.validRange: 0 to 6 cm jaw opening; least count 0.01, 0.005 or 0.002 cm
scientificValidation.unitSystem: cm for all lengths, cm³ for volume
edgeCases: Jaw opening below one least count cannot be resolved — blocked
Zero error larger than the reading itself gives a negative corrected value
A 50-division vernier resolves 1.234 cm where a 10-division one reads 1.23 cm
Fewer than three readings gives no meaningful mean — blocked
expectedBehaviour: M.S.R. + V.S.R. × L.C. always reconstructs the total reading exactly
Positive zero error lowers the corrected reading, negative raises it
Mean of repeated readings converges on the true dimension
Volume scales as the cube of the diameter for a sphere
